contextTopics.label: Russlands Krieg gegen die Ukraine
background: Russland überfiel die Ukraine am 24. Februar 2022 in vollem Umfang. Vorausgegangen war die Annexion der Krim im März 2014 und der von Russland unterstützte bewaffnete Konflikt im Donbas ab April 2014.

Die UN-Generalversammlung verurteilte den Angriff am 2. März 2022 mit 141 zu 5 Stimmen und forderte den sofortigen Rückzug. Die EU, die USA und weitere Staaten verhängten seither mehrere Sanktionspakete.
Der Internationale Strafgerichtshof erließ im März 2023 einen Haftbefehl gegen Wladimir Putin wegen der Verschleppung ukrainischer Kinder.
Österreich ist militärisch neutral, beteiligt sich aber an den EU-Sanktionen und leistet humanitäre Hilfe. Waffenlieferungen erfolgen nicht.

contextTopics.label: Krieg in Gaza und im Nahen Osten
background: Die Hamas verübte am 7. Oktober 2023 einen Großangriff auf Israel mit rund 1.200 Toten und etwa 250 Verschleppten. Israel begann daraufhin eine großangelegte Militäroperation im Gazastreifen.
Der Konflikt reicht weit zurück: Israel wurde 1948 gegründet, es folgten mehrere Kriege mit arabischen Nachbarstaaten. Der Gazastreifen wird seit 2007 von der Hamas kontrolliert.
Der Internationale Gerichtshof befasst sich seit Dezember 2023 mit einer Klage Südafrikas wegen mutmaßlichen Völkermords; ein Urteil in der Hauptsache steht aus.

Zahlenangaben zu Opfern stammen je nach Meldung von unterschiedlichen Stellen — der von der Hamas geführten Gesundheitsbehörde, israelischen Angaben oder UN-Organisationen. Sie sind selten unabhängig überprüfbar.

contextTopics.label: Handelskonflikte und Zölle
background: Die USA erhoben ab 2018 unter Präsident Trump Zölle auf Stahl, Aluminium und zahlreiche chinesische Waren. China antwortete mit Gegenzöllen. Teile davon blieben auch unter der Nachfolgeregierung bestehen.
Die EU ist als Zollunion für die Handelspolitik ihrer Mitgliedsstaaten zuständig — Österreich verhandelt also nicht selbst, sondern die Europäische Kommission.
Zölle wirken auf zwei Wegen: Sie verteuern eingeführte Waren für Verbraucher im Einfuhrland und treffen Exporteure im Ausland. Wer die Kosten trägt, ist wirtschaftswissenschaftlich umstritten.

contextTopics.label: Inflation und Zinspolitik der EZB
background: Die Europäische Zentralbank hat als vorrangiges Ziel Preisstabilität, definiert als 2 Prozent Inflation mittelfristig. Sie steuert darüber den Leitzins für den gesamten Euroraum.
Nach Jahren mit Null- und Negativzinsen begann die EZB im Juli 2022 mit Zinserhöhungen, um die stark gestiegene Inflation zu dämpfen — ausgelöst unter anderem durch Energiepreise und Lieferengpässe.

Österreich lag bei der Inflationsrate über Jahre über dem Euroraum-Durchschnitt. Die Gründe dafür sind umstritten; genannt werden unter anderem Energiepreise, Mietanpassungen und der Gastronomiesektor.

contextTopics.label: Klimapolitik und Klimaziele
background: Im Pariser Abkommen von 2015 verpflichteten sich fast alle Staaten, die Erderwärmung deutlich unter 2 Grad gegenüber dem vorindustriellen Niveau zu halten und 1,5 Grad anzustreben.
Die EU hat sich auf Klimaneutralität bis 2050 festgelegt und Zwischenziele für 2030 beschlossen. Österreich strebt Klimaneutralität bis 2040 an — früher als die EU-Vorgabe.

Der Weltklimarat IPCC fasst regelmäßig den Forschungsstand zusammen. Dass die Erwärmung überwiegend menschengemacht ist, gilt dort als gesichert; umstritten sind Tempo, regionale Folgen und Gegenmaßnahmen.

contextTopics.label: Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz
background: Die Europäische Kommission legte 2021 den Entwurf für den AI Act vor, die weltweit erste umfassende Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz. Er stuft Anwendungen nach Risiko ein und verbietet einige ganz.
Das Gesetz gilt für Anbieter, die ihre Systeme im EU-Markt anbieten — unabhängig davon, wo sie sitzen. Die Pflichten greifen gestaffelt über mehrere Jahre.
Kritik kommt von zwei Seiten: Teilen der Industrie, die Wettbewerbsnachteile befürchten, und Bürgerrechtsorganisationen, denen die Ausnahmen für Sicherheitsbehörden zu weit gehen.

contextTopics.label: Österreichische Innenpolitik
background: Österreich ist eine parlamentarische Demokratie. Der Nationalrat mit 183 Abgeordneten wird alle fünf Jahre gewählt; die Regierung braucht dessen Vertrauen.
Der Bundespräsident wird direkt gewählt, ernennt die Regierung und kann sie entlassen — eine Befugnis, die historisch selten genutzt wurde.
Untersuchungsausschüsse sind ein Minderheitsrecht: Ein Viertel der Abgeordneten kann einen einsetzen, ohne Zustimmung der Mehrheit.

contextTopics.label: Raiffeisen Bank International
background: Die Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI) ist eine der größten Banken Österreichs mit Schwerpunkt in Zentral- und Osteuropa. Sie ging 2010 aus der Fusion von RZB-Teilen und Raiffeisen International hervor.
Der Raiffeisen-Sektor ist genossenschaftlich aufgebaut: lokale Raiffeisenbanken, darüber Landesbanken, darüber die RBI. Diese Struktur erklärt, warum Entscheidungen oft mehrere Ebenen betreffen.
Das Russland-Geschäft der RBI steht seit dem Angriff auf die Ukraine unter besonderer Beobachtung von EZB und US-Behörden. Ein Rückzug wurde mehrfach angekündigt und verzögerte sich.

items.title: How to Decide Whether to Continue an Initiative in the Age of AI
items.summary: AI can shorten the time it takes to turn a proposal into something we can test. Once an initiative is underway, how should a manager decide whether to keep going, change course, or stop? I look at two things: the goal we’re aiming for and the evidence we use as a compass. Are We Getting Closer, and Is the Goal Still Right? First, I look at whether the initiative is moving us toward the goal and whether the goal is still worth pursuing. The same change can mean different things depending on what we’re trying to achieve. Comparing what happened with what we planned says little about why the work is worth doing in the first place. Use Business Value as a Compass Next, I look at how business value is changing. Are we delivering more value in the market? Is our organization getting better at delivering and improving that value? Both questions tell us what evidence to look for. It’s hard to establish how much value an individual feature created or which outcome a particular activity contributed to. When a leading indicator moves, the link to a later change in a lagging indicator is still a hypothesis. Comparing teams by productivity or by the value they generate, or checking whether work went according to plan, does little to answer whether an initiative should continue. This way of thinking comes from Evidence-Based Management (EBM). We set a direction, gather evidence through experiments, and use what we learn to revisit the goal or change our approach. EBM examines market value through Current Value (CV) and Unrealized Value (UV). It examines organizational capability through Ability to Innovate (A2I) and Time-to-Market (T2M). Read the EBM Guide Figure 1. The path to a goal can involve dead ends and backtracking. Evidence about market value and organizational capability helps us decide where to go next. Inspired by Figure 2 of the Evidence-Based Management Guide. Look at What Might Change and When The time it takes to see a response varies by initiative. Consider where a change might show up and when you might reasonably expect to see it. AI can speed up implementation. Customers and markets respond on their own timelines. At the outset, we may be unsure about both the goal and what to look for as a sign of value. Use the feedback you get to reconsider where you’re heading and what evidence you rely on to guide you. Set a Date to Review What You’ve Learned There’s a limit to how long we can wait for feedback. For each initiative, consider what might change and when you could reasonably observe it. Use that estimate to set a review date. This idea draws on the Agile Kata practice of setting an achieve-by date for the next target condition. Scrum uses recurring Sprints of a fixed length. Here, the review date is an opportunity to look at what has happened so far and decide what to do next. Set it for the initiative at hand and move it if the feedback and evidence you have gathered warrant more time. Expore Agile Kata Read the Scrum Guide Make the Decision When the Goal and Evidence Support It Deciding whether to continue, change course, or stop requires a goal that still makes sense and evidence that helps us judge progress toward it. Looking again at the goal helps us interpret the changes we’ve observed. Those changes can also prompt us to reconsider why we’re pursuing the goal. We need both to make a sound decision. On the review date, look at what you’ve learned so far. If you have enough evidence to decide, choose whether to continue, change course, or stop. If further observation would help, say what you want to find out and set the next review date. If you have to make a decision now, make clear which evidence you’re relying on. Figure 2. Bring feedback from experiments into the review. Inspired by the Experiment Loop in Figure 1 of the Evidence-Based Management Guide and the Agile Kata approach to setting dates.

items.title: The Frame Holds the Picture. How You Paint it is Up to You.
items.summary: From the Scrum Guide: "Scrum is a lightweight framework that helps people, teams and organizations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems." The Cambridge Dictionary defines a framework as "a system of rules, ideas, or beliefs that is used to plan or decide something." Look at what that definition leaves out. There are no instructions in it. A system of rules helps you plan and decide; it doesn't tell you how to carry out the plan. In almost every training and coaching assignment, I get the same two questions. How should we prioritize our Product Backlog? How should we write our user stories? The Scrum Guide answers neither, and that's deliberate. In class I split the word in two. A frame, in Cambridge's words, is "a border that encloses and supports a picture, mirror, etc." It holds the picture and supports it. It doesn't care what the picture shows. What a team uses Scrum for is the team's choice, whether that's software or a marketing campaign. Then there's the work. You can make a picture in oil, in watercolor, with a camera or with a pencil. The frame doesn't choose for you. What you want to make usually guides you in how you make it. The same goes for ordering a Product Backlog or describing what the team will build. The people using the framework decide the how, as long as the framework's rules, ideas and beliefs are used. When the Guide doesn't answer the how, teams often look elsewhere. They borrow a popular technique and start calling it Scrum. Story points, user stories, a fixed Retrospective format. When the borrowed technique doesn't fit their picture, Scrum gets the blame for a choice it never made. Leaving the how with the team pays off. McKinsey found that organizations that empower employees to make decisions are about 3.9 times more likely to be top performers. The frame only delivers that when the team picks its own how, not when a manager or a tool fills it in for them. Try this with your team: List two or three of your current how-to's, such as how you order the Product Backlog, how you write backlog items and how you estimate. For each one, ask: did we choose this because of what we're making, or did we take it over from somewhere? Then ask: if we started from the product we want to make, would we choose the same way? Keep what passes, and pick one to change as an experiment next Sprint. I hope you find value in these short articles and if you are looking for more clarifications, feel free to make contact. Don't want to miss any of these blog posts? Have the “The Scrum Guide Explored” series weekly in your mailbox . Wishing you an inspiring read and a wonderful journey. Scrum on! Image

items.title: KI-Einführungsfehler: Warum Ihr erfolgreiches KI-Pilotprojekt kein Grund zum Skalieren ist 🇩🇪
items.summary: In Kürze: Sieben typische KI-Einführungsfehler und wie man sie vermeidet These : Dieser Artikel erklärt sieben KI-Einführungsfehler, die auf ein erfolgreiches KI-Pilotprojekt folgen, von nicht einsatzbereiten Daten über überlastete Prüfer bis zu verfrühten Kürzungen, und wie Praktiker den Qualitätsstandard festlegen, die Evidenz sammeln und die Ergebnisse überprüfen, bevor sie die KI-Einführung über das Pilotprojekt hinaus skalieren. Ihr KI-Pilotprojekt hat funktioniert: Die Demo hat den Lenkungsausschuss beeindruckt, die Zeitersparnis auf der PowerPoint-Folie sah fantastisch aus, und der Projektsponsor entwirft bereits das Budget für den Rollout. Das Pilotprojekt hat jedoch eine engere Frage beantwortet, als das Budget vorsieht. Es hat gezeigt, dass die Technologie die Aufgabe unter Testbedingungen erledigen kann: mit sauberen Daten, einem handverlesenen Team und einem Prozess, der hauptsächlich in den Standardarbeitsanweisungen dokumentiert ist. Zwei Fragen bleiben offen, und niemand hat Beweise dafür gesammelt: ob gewöhnliche Teams den Workflow zuverlässig betreiben können und ob sich eine Ausweitung über das Pilotprojekt hinaus auszahlt. Im Folgenden finden Sie sieben KI-Einführungsfehler, die sich 2026 in traditionellen Organisationen immer wieder zeigen, jeweils mit einem Warnsignal, das Sie noch diese Woche prüfen können, und einer Gegenmaßnahme, sowie fünf Fragen für die Skalierungsentscheidung selbst. Sie müssen nicht über das Budget verfügen, um sie nutzen zu können. Denn der Beweis, den eine Skalierungsentscheidung erfordert, kommt von den Menschen, die der Arbeit am nächsten sind: Sie einigen sich vor dem Versuch auf den Qualitätsstandard, zum Beispiel mit der KI-Definition of Done, sammeln die Beweise während des Workflows und überprüfen die Delegation im Zeitverlauf mit einem KI-Delegations-Audit. Spoiler-Alarm für erfahrene agile Praktiker: Wenn Sie eine agile Transformation miterlebt haben, werden Ihnen die meisten dieser Fehler vertraut vorkommen. Die Geschichte reimt sich, und KI bildet, wie zuvor Agile, keine Ausnahme. Image Transparenzhinweis : Ich habe das Buch von Charniak und McDermott über „Artificial Intelligence“ vor Jahrzehnten gelesen; selbstverständlich nutze ich KI für Recherche, Übersetzungen, Korrekturlesen, das Hinterfragen von Spannungsbögen und Artikelstrukturen, die Erstellung von Artefakten wie Grafiken sowie für Zusammenfassungen. KI ist ein Produktionswerkzeug, kein Ersatz für das Denken. 🗞 Shall I notify you about articles like this one? Awesome! You can sign up here for the ‘Food for Agile Thought’ newsletter and join 35,000-plus subscribers . Das KI-Pilotprojekt war erfolgreich, und genau darin liegt das Problem Ein kleines, gut konzipiertes KI-Experiment, das scheitert, ist günstig: Es kostet ein paar Wochen, ein kleines Budget und etwas Stolz, und meist lernt die Organisation dabei etwas über ihre Daten und Prozesse. Ein erfolgreiches Pilotprojekt kann dagegen teuer werden, weil es dem Sponsor scheinbar Evidenz für einen Rollout liefert, den das Pilotprojekt nie getestet hat. Sobald der Rollout beginnt, trifft die KI auf die Organisation, wie sie tatsächlich funktioniert, und aus dem erwarteten Ergebnis entstehen Eskalationen, Workarounds und Änderungsanträge, die niemand auf der ursprünglichen PowerPoint-Folie festgehalten hat. Nichts davon macht das KI-Pilotprojekt wertlos. Eine eng gefasste technische Hypothese unter kontrollierten Bedingungen zu testen, ist legitim, und kuratierte Daten sowie motivierte Freiwillige können genau der richtige Rahmen dafür sein. Der Fehler tritt einen Schritt später auf, wenn die Organisation das Ergebnis nutzt, um eine Frage zu beantworten, die das Pilotprojekt nie gestellt hat. Hinter „Das KI-Pilotprojekt hat funktioniert“ verbergen sich drei Fragen, und jede braucht andere Evidenz: Kann die Technologie diese Aufgabe erledigen? Nachweis: Leistung unter festgelegten Testbedingungen, also das, was ein Pilotprojekt üblicherweise liefert. Können gewöhnliche Teams diesen Workflow zuverlässig betreiben? Nachweis: Ergebnisse bei repräsentativen Fällen, die Ausnahmen, die Supportanfragen und die Zeit, die Menschen mit der Vorbereitung des Inputs und der Prüfung des Outputs verbringen. Sollten wir das KI-Pilotprojekt skalieren? items.title: I Do Continuous Delivery, Why Should I Sprint?
items.summary: Originally published at Engineering Leadership on 13 July 2020 as I do continuous deliver, why should I Sprint? Updated on 18 March 2024. Many folks believe that a Sprint is an arbitrary length of time in which you create and release software. They look at their continuous delivery pipeline and say to themselves; “Why would I limit myself to shipping only once every two weeks?” UPDATE: Scrum .org just posted my Scrum Tapas - Scrum and Continuous Delivery which is posted inline below. To that I say: “Where in the Scrum Guide does it say that you can’t release every day?” You will not find it, I know as I have looked. I work with many teams that release software on a continuous delivery model of everything from a few hours, to a few days, and often on-demand. Can you say that they are not doing Scrum? Of course not. So why would you want a Sprint at all? A Sprint enshrines your empirical process by providing a maximum delivery cadence It increases communication and alignment It Adds some predictability to the unpredictable nature of software by evening the batch sizes. A Sprint is a container for planning! As far as the Scrum Guide is concerned you must deliver working software at least every 30 days, but there is nothing to stop you doing it more frequently than that. Indeed continuous delivery and Scrum go together quite well in my experience. A Sprint enshrines inspect and adapt by containing your other feedback loops: Sprint Planning - Inspect the Backlog and Adapt the plan for the next Sprint Daily Scrum - Inspect progress and adapt the plan for the next 24hours. Sprint Review - Inspect the Increment and adapt the Backlog Sprint Retrospective - Inspect the Sprint and adapt the process. Without a Sprint when would you bring all this together? The Sprint makes the effort required to pull your work together and create a Done increment of software mandatory. It is absolutely crucial to understand that if you don’t at least have working software that meets your definition of done by the end of the Sprint then you are not doing Scrum. If you are an awesome disciplined team then by all means do something that looks a little more like Kanban , but if you don’t have the discipline to follow the rules of Scrum, how would you expect Kanban to work. Communication & Alignment An additional benefit of Sprinting is that it gives a cadence that your management, and other dependant teams, can follow easily. If you are coordinating work, then having a common frame of reference, Sprint 231, will aid in communication. Creates Predictability Software is inherently unpredictable. The standard deviation between the amount of work required for seemingly similar tasks is so big that it is very difficult to gain predictability. A Sprint creates an artificial batch of a fixed size (or at least less varied) with a time boxed Sprint so that you can create that cadence of predictability. Conclusion A Sprint is a container for planning rather than releasing and while Scrum requires that you have a working increment of software at least every Sprint, there is nothing to stop you doing it more often. Indeed the recommendation from Scrum.org is that you not only ship your software at least every 30 days, you should endeavour to do so more often. Scrum.org recently changed its mantra from “Improve the profession of software development ” to “Improve the profession of software delivery” to start to enshrine the idea that delivery, to your customers, is no longer optional to get significant actionable feedback that you can reflect on. In short, while the Scrum Guide does not explicitly state it, it is no longer optional to ship your software to production at least every 30 days if you want to stay competitive and build the software that your users deserve. Subscribe on Engineering Leadership for Martin's posts, including those not on Scrum.org, and for updated editions of articles like this one.

items.title: 🇨🇵 Votre prochain concurrent peut naître ce week-end. Et maintenant ?
items.summary: Image Pendant des décennies, construire un logiciel demandait du budget, des équipes et du temps. C’était une barrière à l’entrée, et pour beaucoup d’entreprises un avantage confortable. Cette barrière est tombée et les preuves sont là. ▪️ Le code : Selon le rapport GitHub Octoverse 2026 , les commits ont atteint 34,3 milliards sur douze mois, plus du triple de 2024. Depuis juin, environ 55 % des commits proviennent de dépôts créés dans l’année. En septembre, plus de 40 % des pull requests ont commencé par une première proposition d’un agent IA. ▪️ Les outils : Lovable revendique plus de 60 millions de projets créés depuis son lancement fin 2024. ▪️ Le web : Selon Verisign , le nombre de noms de domaine a atteint 411,6 millions au troisième trimestre 2026, soit +8,7 % sur un an, contre seulement +1,2 % fin 2024. Les nouveaux enregistrements en .com et .net sont passés de 10,6 à 13,1 millions en un an. ▪️ Les entreprises : Dans l’enquête State of AI 2026 de McKinsey (1 719 répondants), 32 % déclarent que leur organisation a renoncé à acheter au moins un logiciel ou une fonctionnalité parce que des agents de code permettaient de les construire en interne. Ce chiffre monte à 41 % dans le secteur technologique. Les marchés financiers eux-mêmes s’inquiètent : début février 2026, près de 1 000 milliards de dollars de capitalisation se sont évaporés des valeurs américaines des logiciels et services, sur fond de craintes liées à l’IA ( Reuters ). Certes, un nom de domaine n’est pas un produit, un commit n’est pas de la valeur, et une chute boursière ne prouve pas une disparition des revenus. Mais ces signaux racontent une transformation : construire n’est plus réservé à ceux qui ont des moyens. Votre prochain concurrent peut naître ce week-end 🧑‍💻 C’est la conséquence la plus inconfortable : lancer une alternative ne nécessite plus forcément une équipe, un budget conséquent ni plusieurs trimestres. L’un des exemples les plus frappants de 2026 est celui de Brandon Thomas. Ce développeur expérimenté a publié sept applications open source écrites en Rust avec l’aide d’une IA, reproduisant une partie des fonctionnalités de Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign et Acrobat. Il s’est ensuite attaqué à Microsoft avec WordCraft, DeckCraft et GridCraft, trois alternatives à Word, PowerPoint et Excel. Evidemment PhotoCraft n’est pas encore un véritable remplaçant de Photoshop pour un usage professionnel. En huit jours, les sept dépôts liés à Adobe avaient cumulé plus de 42 000 étoiles sur GitHub. Un développeur qui attire autant d’attention face à deux des plus grands éditeurs du monde. David contre Goliath à l'ère de l'IA ! C’est précisément ce qui change : produire une alternative impressionnante devient rapide. Construire un produit fiable, adopté et durable reste une autre histoire. La vraie menace n’est pas qu’un inconnu remplace votre produit un lundi matin. C’est que le nombre de concurrents potentiels augmente considérablement. Et qu’un seul, en ciblant une niche mal servie, peut suffire à attirer vos clients ou à remettre vos prix en question. Alors, comment se démarquer ? 🎯 Si tout le monde peut construire, la fabrication seule ne suffit plus à vous protéger. Voici ce qui, selon moi, reste défendable, et que chaque Product Manager devrait dorénavant considérer. 1. Accéder aux utilisateurs avant les autres. L’exemple le plus parlant vient d’Apple, Google lui a versé environ 20 milliards de dollars en 2022 pour rester le moteur de recherche par défaut sur ses appareils. Une somme considérable pour une chose : être là où se trouvent les utilisateurs. La distribution est un avantage concurrentiel souvent sous-estimé. Un concurrent peut reproduire vos fonctionnalités, mais pas instantanément vos canaux d’acquisition, votre base installée, vos partenariats ou votre position dans un écosystème. La question est simple : quels accès à vos utilisateurs un nouvel entrant ne peut-il pas reproduire en un week-end ? 2. S’ancrer dans le quotidien de vos clients. Un produit difficile à remplacer n’est pas nécessairement celui qui possède le plus de fonctionnalités. C’est souvent celui dont le remplacement bouleverserait les habitudes, les données, les intégrations et les processus. Les habitudes protègent, mais les coûts de change peuvent protéger davantage. Changer d’outil devient autrement plus compliqué lorsqu’il faut aussi modifier la façon dont une organisation travaille. Et lorsque la valeur d’un produit grandit avec son réseau d’utilisateurs ou de partenaires, la copie devient encore plus difficile. 3. Apprendre plus vite que les autres. Des données propriétaires, gouvernées et enrichies en continu peuvent constituer un avantage précieux. Mais les posséder ne suffit pas. Ce qui compte, c’est ce qu’elles vous permettent d’apprendre, et la vitesse à laquelle cet apprentissage améliore votre produit. Un concurrent peut copier votre interface. Il aura plus de mal à reproduire trois ans de…

items.title: What an Effective Sprint Review Looks Like
items.summary: The vast majority of the Sprint Reviews I attend are painfully ineffective. They are often snooze-fests that stakeholders eventually stop showing up for altogether. The direct consequence is that you, as the Product Owner, end up updating everyone individually afterward. That takes loads of extra time, creates endless alignment loops, and completely misses the point of agility and focus. A Sprint Review is not a demo to show off how hard the team has worked. Nor is it a sales pitch where you put on a good show. A Sprint Review is a working session with one single goal: gathering feedback on the direction and state of the product. If you turn it into a laundry list of fifty completed tickets, you’re missing the point entirely. If nobody shows up, it’s not important enough I see plenty of product owners struggling with stakeholders who don't show up. That requires a bit of honest self-reflection: if nobody shows up, you’re probably not working on things that are important enough. Let that sink in for a moment. Image Sprints are expensive. Just because we can build faster these days doesn’t make it any cheaper to build the wrong thing. Yet, I still see people get shocked when they calculate the actual cost of a single sprint. Your stakeholders do walk into a Sprint Review with that expectation: they want to see something worth at least a decent mid-range car. Instead, they often leave disappointed because all we did was fix a typo or move a button three pixels to the right. Stop ‘completing the sprint’ I always chuckle a little when I hear Product Owners say they ‘completed’ or ‘made’ the last sprint. From the perspective of a ‘scrum hippie’, that’s just hilarious. A Sprint is a timebox; it’s going to end no matter what. The only thing you have to do to ‘make’ a sprint is keep breathing until the clock runs out. All jokes aside: the moment a team celebrates that, all my alarm bells go off. It means the team is primarily focused on being as productive as possible and churning out maximum output. If you manage based on ‘completing the Sprint’ as your metric of success, you lose sight of your accountability for maximizing value delivery. Stakeholders will start judging you on checking off tickets within two weeks, rather than taking responsibility for what actually goes live and the impact it makes. Is output your only yardstick? Then your stakeholders will hold you to that standard! That severely limits your team’s effectiveness and for you as a PO, that goes double. The real goal: gathering feedback (even if they storm out) The goal of the Sprint Review is simple: gather feedback. What do your stakeholders, customers, and users think of what’s on the table? If they storm out of the room, but they told you what they liked and disliked about it, then it was a successful Sprint Review, as long as you captured how they feel about it. So make sure the right people are in the room. Too often, we measure the success of a Sprint Review by the decibels produced by our cheering squad (yes, your stakeholders!). Applause at the end of a Sprint Review is great, sure, but that’s not why you’re doing it. A few years ago, I worked with a team where this happened. I quickly shut the door and asked: “That’s lovely applause at the end, but why did you clap? Are you glad it’s over, or are you glad you saw something ‘moving’ that resembles a finished product?” Nobody was allowed to leave the room until they explained why they had applauded. My approach might have been a bit extreme, but my point is this: as a Product Owner, it is your job to make sure you get that feedback, even when it isn't positive! Set this up during sprint planning An effective review starts in Sprint Planning. That’s where you take care of two things: Pick two to three items for feedback: Decide during Sprint Planning which two or three items you want to present to your stakeholders in the Sprint Review. This allows the entire Scrum Team to prepare: what is the context, what did we actually deliver, what are we trying to achieve with it, and what specific feedback do we want to receive? Demand the same commitment from your stakeholders: We ask developers for commitment. You are allowed to expect that exact same commitment from stakeholders. Do they desperately want something built, yet they can’t be bothered to show up or send someone with a mandate? Then feel free to ask them how important it really is. Check that upfront, not afterward. In fact, at a major supermarket chain, this escalated massively when we refused to pick up an item because the stakeholder didn't find it important enough to give feedback on the problem we were trying to solve for him. Because honestly, if they don’t care enough about it, why should we? What a good Sprint Review looks like No half-hour demo where you showcase fifty things. The goal of the Sprint Review is to look together at whether you’re on the right track and examine the state of the product. You don’t need PowerPoint…

items.title: How Can Managers Support Team Learning in the Age of AI?
items.summary: AI can reduce the time it takes to create code and documents. But if we focus only on how much a team produces or how quickly it works, we risk losing sight of what the team has learned and what has changed for its customers. For a team using AI, a crucial part of its work is experimenting and making decisions. Managers, in turn, need to create an environment in which the team can keep learning in pursuit of the outcomes customers desire. Learning in Pursuit of a Mission Whether a team is learning depends on what it needs to learn. Its mission gives it a direction, and the team needs to be able to decide for itself what it should learn along the way. The manager who has provided that mission should look at whether the team is moving toward it. The team's approach may differ from the one the manager initially had in mind. Even so, the manager can assess whether the team is working toward goals it has set for itself and conducting experiments along the way. It is also important to look at what facts the team has discovered through those experiments and how it has used them in its next decisions. Image Figure 1. Team learning toward a mission, supported by a manager In situations of high uncertainty and complexity, managers themselves often do not know the right answer, even if, like anyone else, they may find that hard to admit. In those situations, the team's own decisions and experiments should take precedence over following the particular tasks a manager had in mind. Use AI to Support Experiments and Decisions AI is well suited to helping teams collect and evaluate data and evidence for their decisions. Code generation, for example, can be seen as one means of conducting an experiment. The team's important work goes beyond showing what it has produced: What did the experiment reveal, and how will that inform the next decision? That also means checking what can be treated as fact, including the output of AI. In a study published by Anthropic in 2026, 52 developers worked on a task involving a Python library that was new to them. On a test immediately afterward, the AI-assisted group scored an average of 50%, compared with 67% for the group without AI. These results came from a particular task and a short-term test. Participants also used AI in different ways, and the results do not directly establish its effect on a team's long-term capabilities. Read the Anthropic study A separate preprint analyzing 23 studies found no statistically significant overall effect on programming learning outcomes. Ten of those studies contributed to the learning-outcome analysis. The analysis covered studies published from 2019 through 2025; it also cites the 2026 Anthropic study in its references. We need to consider how AI is used and the context in which it is used when assessing its effects on learning. Read the analysis of AI use in programming From Output Volume to Customer Outcomes Managers should ensure that teams are not judged solely by activity or output measures, such as the amount of code produced or the number of features built. If work continues to be evaluated through the same old lens, teams will continue to feel the same pressure. They need an environment where they can focus on building toward outcomes that customers and users value. That requires building relationships with stakeholders and enabling teams to learn quickly and repeatedly. Working toward desired customer outcomes also affects an internal outcome: team morale. As this engine develops, it can support greater team autonomy and continuous improvement. Managers need to communicate the value of this way of working and help build the relationships that sustain it, through dialogue both within the organization and with stakeholders. Discuss the Evidence for Building to Plan Stakeholders may ask a team to build many features according to a plan. When they do, we should examine the evidence that doing so will lead to what customers actually want. Without that evidence, we cannot take the relationship between output volume or plan completion and customer outcomes for granted. We need to explain why a different way of making sense of the situation is needed and open a dialogue. The Cynefin framework offers one way to do this. It helps us make sense of a situation and consider how to make decisions. Is the situation clear, complicated and in need of expert analysis, or complex and best understood through experimentation? Start with sense-making: develop a shared understanding of the situation with stakeholders. Explore the Cynefin framework In that dialogue, clarify business goals and the outcomes customers desire, and consider the balance between them. At the same time, ask how both may change as markets, user needs, and technology evolve. Image Figure 2. items.title: The Last Minute of Planning is the One that Matters.
items.summary: Image Think back to the last problem that blindsided the people at the top. The status that was green all quarter and then snapped. The deadline that was fine until, suddenly, it wasn't. Now think about the debrief. One after another, people admitted they'd had a feeling. "I was a bit worried about that dependency." "I wasn't sure the estimate held." "Honestly, I thought we were cutting it close." The information wasn't missing. It was in the building the whole time. It just never made it into a decision while there was still time to act on it. I've seen that change inside the last minute of a planning session the team was already having. No extra meeting, no added time. At a large agricultural-machinery manufacturer, the first round surfaced a critical dependency on another team that nobody had put on the table. It changed how the two teams worked: where that team had been doing the whole job, the team I worked with did the work and they validated the process had been applied correctly. That's the friction we call the Known Surprise, and it isn't a discipline problem. It's what happens when the quiet worry has nowhere safe and normal to go until it's already a crisis. The good news is that the repair for it is almost embarrassingly small. It fits in the last minute of a meeting you're already having. Why reality shows up late People don't hide concerns because they're dishonest. They hide them because surfacing a problem early can look like negativity, or like not being on top of your work, so the safe move is to wait until you're certain, and by the time you are, it has already become an incident. The gap this creates is bigger than most leaders realize, because they're on the wrong side of it. In a 2025 Axios HQ study, leaders rated their own internal communication far higher than their people did, a gap of about 30 points on whether the message was even clear. Both sides of that are self-reported, which is exactly what makes it useful: it doesn't measure how good the communication was, it measures how differently the two levels experienced the same messages. The person at the top feels aligned. The people doing the work are holding concerns the top never hears. And it isn't a few people staying quiet: roughly 6 in 10 employees say they're afraid to speak up at work, according to a 2026 Radical Candor survey. When that's the water the team swims in, "just tell me sooner" does nothing. You have to make surfacing the worry the normal, expected, low-cost thing to do. The repair: a Risk Round-Robin Here's the move. It's one of several that can rebuild Reality Transparency, and it's the one worth trying first because it costs almost nothing. At the end of your next planning session, in the last minute before everyone closes their laptops, run a round. Every person names the single biggest unsurfaced concern they're holding, even a half-formed one. You write them down. That's the whole thing. Why it could help: it forces the weak signals into shared understanding before they need certainty or a reason to exist. A worry that would otherwise wait until it was undeniable gets said out loud while it's still small enough to act on. Nobody has to be braver for this to work. The concern simply gets a scheduled, expected place to land, so saying it out loud stops being an act of courage. A possible sign it's working: two concerns a week start surfacing that the team couldn't see before, and at least one of them changes a decision while it's still early and cheap. The watch-out, because every repair has one: if the same generic worries come up every week, it's turned into ritual. Rotate the prompt, biggest delivery worry, biggest quality worry, biggest stakeholder worry, or it stops being real. Run it as a probe One honest caveat, because this system doesn't sell silver bullets. The Risk Round-Robin is not the answer to the Known Surprise. Treat it as an experiment you run and inspect. If a month of it surfaces nothing real, that's information too: the fear is deeper than a one-minute round can reach, and the fundamental underneath, Reality Transparency, needs a different move aimed at what surfacing a problem actually costs on your team. But most teams are surprised how much a single protected minute pulls into the light. It's the cheapest test you can run of whether reality is reaching you on time. So, one question before your next planning session: what's the biggest worry on your team that nobody has said out loud yet? Take the two-minute self-diagnostic → https://www.fundamentalsfirst.eu/self-diagnostic Your framework isn't broken. Your fundamentals are. Scrum on!

items.title: From 5 Teams to More Than 100: How a Pharma Field Organization Scaled Agility
items.summary: A field organization started with five cross-functional pilot teams. A few years later it had more than a hundred, and each therapeutic area had found its own way of working. It didn't scale because of a master plan or deployment roadmap. It scaled because each phase delivered new information about what works. In the second post of this series , I described four ways pharma companies adopt agility, and promised a few case studies. This is the first one. On that map, it started as a function-led transformation in a commercial organization. It's also the organization I briefly mentioned in the first post : the one that moved from a traditional sales structure to cross-functional teams, and then kept changing shape for the following two years. As with every case in this series, I have removed names, dates and details that could identify the company. The story and the lessons are real. The starting point The company was a large global pharma company, and the organization in question was its field force: medical representatives, supported by marketing, medical and other functions at headquarters. The reason to change was not a vague "we should be more agile". It was that the environment had become more complex. The needs of the healthcare system and all its stakeholders (patients, doctors, etc.) were more varied and constantly changing (digitalization, new limits on doctors' working hours, etc.). Decisions made once a year at headquarters were often out of date by the time they reached the field. The people closest to customers needed to be able to decide and adjust faster, and more locally. The way the organization worked made that difficult: Function first. Sales, digital marketing, medical, and other supporting functions each had their own goals and their own plans, and they met mostly at handoffs. Annual and semi-annual planning. Plans were set at the start of the cycle and executed, with little room to learn and adjust in between. Top-down goals. Targets came from above. Field teams were accountable for delivering them, not for shaping them. This weakened ownership and limited the ability to tap into the MRs' wisdom and insights from the field. Physician-centric engagement. Most activity was organized around visits to individual doctors, while the decisions that matter for patients involve many more people. The leadership's ambition was to improve patient outcomes, customer value and commercial results at the same time, in a few priority therapeutic areas. They didn't believe the existing structure could do all three at once. What changed The change worked on three things at once. Looking back, I think that matters more than any single practice they adopted. Mindset: patients at the center, teams trusted to decide, and accountable for continuous improvement. Ways of working: short cycles built around hypotheses ("if we do this with these customers, we expect that "), regular feedback from customers, and Sprints replacing most of the annual and semi-annual plans. Organization design: cross-functional teams organized by area, a national team to coordinate and support them, goals shared across functions, and a new incentive scheme to match. Together, these amounted to five shifts: From accountability held by leaders to empowerment across the organization From goals set function by function to shared goals across functions From physician-centric engagement to engagement with all the stakeholders around the patient From annual and semi-annual planning to short cycles of hypothesis and test From a product-centric organization to a patient-centric organization None of these shifts is new in itself. What made the difference, in my view, is that they were pursued together. Teams that are asked to run short cycles but are still measured on separate functional targets tend to fall back into the old way quickly. Changing the incentives and the structure at the same time as the ways of working gave the new habits something to hold on to. The operating model The new structure had two layers. Area teams. Each team brought together people from different functions who served the same region. Within the national strategy, they set their own goals and action plans, ran short cycles of hypothesis and test with the customers in their area, and adjusted based on what they learned. National coordination and support. A group of people at headquarters. Their job was not to tell the area teams what to do. They helped the area teams set goals that fit the national strategy, built the capabilities they needed (Scrum mastery, Design Thinking, low-cost experimentation, team facilitation), coordinated across areas, and kept the overhead of the whole system under control. Image The area teams own the decisions about their customers; the national layer owns the boundaries they decide within, and the support they need to do it well. items.title: 🇨🇵 L’IA nous rend du temps : faisons enfin du vrai Product Management
items.summary: Des LLMs impressionnants… et pas (encore) créatifs Soyons clairs : je suis loin d’être un détracteur de l’IA générative. Les LLMs écrivent du code, des tests, de la documentation, des synthèses, et ils le font à une vitesse qui était inimaginable il y a peu. Je les utilise, et vous aussi probablement. Mais plus je les pratique, plus un constat s’impose : ils excellent à produire du plausible. Ils recombinent, reformulent, complètent ce qui existe déjà. Ce qu’ils savent beaucoup moins faire, du moins aujourd’hui, c’est ce que nous faisons naturellement : remarquer ce que personne n’a demandé, relier deux idées qui n’ont rien à voir, ressentir un malaise face à un produit qui « fonctionne » mais qui n’a pas de sens. Ou encore prendre le risque d’un pari. Cette créativité, cette capacité à bâtir une vision à partir d’évidences, l’IA générative actuelle ne l’a pas. Et c’est précisément ce qui devrait nous préoccuper dans la manière dont nous allons utiliser le temps qu’elle nous fait gagner. Le réflexe : toujours plus 🏭 Dans beaucoup de comités de direction, le raisonnement est déjà posé : si l’IA rend les développeurs 30 % plus rapides, il en faut moins. Même production, équipe plus petite, coûts réduits. C’est logique, mais cela suppose que le problème de nos produits était la quantité (output) de fonctionnalités livrées. Nous avons presque tous croisé une feature factory : une roadmap de promesses, un succès mesuré à ce qui part en production plutôt qu’à ce qui change pour l’utilisateur (Melissa Perri parle de build trap). Or, quand construire coûte moins cher, le réflexe naturel est de demander plus. L’IA ne sort pas la feature factory de son piège, elle lui donne un turbo. Et notre excuse préférée, « on n’a pas le temps pour la Discovery », a disparu ! Mais aller plus vite ne mènera pas bien loin 🚤 Même si cette course au volume fonctionnait, elle se heurterait à deux limites. La première : tout le monde accélère. Vos concurrents ont les mêmes outils, les mêmes assistants, la même capacité à générer du code en quelques minutes. La vitesse devient un ticket d’entrée, plus un avantage. Ce qui reste difficile à copier, c’est de savoir quoi construire et pourquoi, et cela nous ramène exactement à ce que les LLMs ne font pas : passer de douze conversations clients à une direction. La seconde : vos clients ne suivent pas forcément. Imaginons une mise en production quotidienne. Beaucoup de produits vivent dans le monde de quelqu’un d’autre, un autre contexte : utilisateurs à former, validations, environnements réglementés, intégrations, équipes support à préparer. Un client qui doit réapprendre ses outils chaque matin ne vit pas la vitesse comme de la valeur, mais comme du bruit. Le rythme utile est fixé par celui qui reçoit, pas par celui qui produit. Alors, ce temps gagné ? 🎯 Si produire plus ne nous distingue pas et que nos clients ne peuvent pas l’absorber, il reste une seule voie : réinvestir le temps libéré là où l’IA est la plus faible, c’est-à-dire dans notre créativité et notre compréhension de l’utilisateur. ▪️ Parler aux clients très régulièrement, pas une fois par trimestre ▪️ Explorer le problème avant de choisir une solution ▪️ Prototyper plusieurs pistes et les confronter à de vraies personnes proche de l'usage, pas vos collègues de bureau. ▪️ Observer, mesurer, analyser, comprendre l’usage réel dès la mise en production L’IA peut accélérer chacune de ces étapes (prototyper une idée en une après-midi rend l’expérimentation bon marché), mais elle ne les remplace pas. Un utilisateur synthétique (persona) n’est pas un client, et un résumé de notes, insights ou feedbacks clients ne vaut pas le fait d’entendre quelqu’un galérer avec votre produit. Et cela concerne toute l’équipe. Dans Scrum, le terme Developers est volontairement large : il couvre toute personne qui contribue à créer le produit avec une expertise et un regard utiles à son évolution (design, recherche, data, qualité, métier, ingénierie…). C’est d’autant plus vrai aujourd’hui. Si une partie du code se génère, ce qui compte devient ce que ces regards apportent : questionner le besoin, challenger une idée, imaginer une expérience. Réduire les équipes au nom de l’efficience, c’est risquer de se priver précisément de celles et ceux qui savent transformer le temps libéré en apprentissage. Pour résumer L’IA va rendre du temps à la plupart des équipes. Ce temps ira quelque part : vers plus de fonctionnalités, ou vers plus de compréhension, de créativité, de vision. Alors posez-vous cette question avec votre équipe : « Si nous avions demain deux fois plus de capacité de livraison, qu’en ferions-nous ? » Si la réponse honnête est « plus de la même chose », alors le problème n’a jamais été la vitesse 🏁 Vous avez aimé cet article ? Je poste régulièrement sur LinkedIn. Suivez-moi ou connectons-nous !

items.title: A Team of AI Agents Needs Scrum, Not a Better Model
items.summary: "Agent = Model + Harness" describes one AI agent well and a team of agents badly. Once agents work together, the defects that matter come from handoffs, shared records and two agents doing the same work. A better model fixes none of those. A team needs a second line: Team = Agents + Coordination. Scrum already supplies the coordination. My own team of AI agents runs on Scrum, and its records show where the defects come from. The formula is right for one agent Vivek Trivedy of LangChain states the formula in exactly those words. He defines the harness as every piece of code, configuration and execution logic that isn't the model (Trivedy, 2026). The model supplies the reasoning and the writing. The harness is the software the agent runs in: it runs the loop, hands the agent its tools and decides what the agent sees. A better model makes one agent write better, and a better harness gets more done from the same model. A team of agents fails at the handoffs Put several agents on one piece of work and someone has to decide which agent takes which task. Every agent also needs the same current copy of the draft. Those are decisions about how the agents work together, so they sit outside any one agent's model. Any Scrum Master has seen the human version: capable Developers who still lose work in the handoff between them. I split coordination into four parts. The Scrum Guide covers each one (Schwaber & Sutherland, 2020): Orchestration is who starts the work and in what order. In Scrum, the Product Owner orders the Product Backlog, the Developers plan the Sprint, and the Scrum Master makes sure the events take place, stay productive and keep to their timebox. Shared state is the record every agent reads and writes. In Scrum, that is the artifacts, such as the Product Backlog and the Sprint Backlog. Protocols are the rules for claiming work and handing it on. Scrum leaves these to the Scrum Team, which is self-managing: it decides who does what, when and how. Governance is what "done" means and who checks it. In Scrum, that is the Definition of Done. The Developers must meet it, and the Scrum Team inspects it at the Sprint Retrospective and changes it as needed. In the full model, each line expands a term from the line above: Team = Agents + Coordination Agents = for each agent: Model + Harness + its role, skills and memory Coordination = Orchestration + Shared state + Protocols + Governance Image Al (short for Aletheia, or "truth" in Ancient Greek) is the Scrum Master of the Relentless Raptors, my agent team. He puts every task on a shared task list and never assigns work. Seven Developers, each a specialist agent, claim tasks themselves: a copywriter, a citations specialist, an image maker, a quality assurance (QA) reviewer, two web builders and a designer. I am the Product Owner. I order the Product Backlog and decide what is released. After every story is Done, a separate AI review reads all of the story's records and traces each error to its cause. I call it the story retrospective; it is not the Sprint Retrospective. The team proposes changes to its own rules and tools, and I approve and make them. Three defects from my team's records that started outside the model 1. Two agents saved over each other's work In late October, the plan for a blog post scheduled two tasks at the same time. The copywriter edited the draft to remove machine-sounding text, and the citations agent added the reference list. Both tasks replace the whole document when they save. The two agents read the draft within seconds of each other. The citations agent saved the references two minutes later. The copywriter saved the edited draft 22 minutes later, built from the copy it read before the references existed, and the reference list was gone. The QA agent found the peer-review gap and restored it. The plan put two whole-document writers side by side, and the save tool never checked whether the document had changed since it was read. The story retrospective recommended a save that rejects a stale copy and a plan check that rejects two writers on one document at once. Neither fix has been built yet. A shared editor that merges changes as people type would have kept both edits; these agents saved whole copies instead. 2. Two agents claimed the same task An agent claims a task the way many Developers sign up for work on their Sprint Backlog: in one place everyone can see, with one name on each task. Each claim creates a lock named after the task, and a second agent that tries the same lock is refused. On 23 October, two agents both took the lock for the same planning task. One filed its lock under the story's name and the other under the planning session's name, so both claims succeeded. Both agents planned the story, and the plan checker refused the result. Two days later the claim rule changed: every lock now goes under the session's name, so two claims on one task meet the same lock and the second is refused. 3. Hand-built handoffs failed…

items.title: The Framework is Not the Point
items.summary: Image I am not sure how many times I have explained to my kids that no, they probably won't use Calculus. And maybe they won't need to know the details of Earth Science. Or how Pride and Prejudice ends. But that's not the point. The point of going to High School is to learn how to learn . How to assimilate and analyze data. To find out what you're capable of and to give you confidence that yes, you can do that thing - whatever "that thing" is for you. Scrum has something in common with Calculus, it turns out. Scrum helps teams learn how to learn. The framework of Scrum isn't the end goal. Just implementing Scrum by itself is helpful, but it's only the beginning. When you implement Scrum, you are implementing a way for the Scrum team to learn how to deliver value better. Here's what I mean. Role clarity empowers the team. The Scrum framework includes three accountabilities : the Product Owner (they decide what the team will work on next), Developers (they deliver the product) and a Scrum Master (they facilitate meetings and improve the adoption of Scrum.) The role clarity that comes from this simple framework is enormous. Whenever I see strife on a team, it often comes from a lack of role clarity. Scrum helps teams get beyond that. When it's clear what your job is, only then you can embrace it and get better at it. Scrum events create a feedback loop. The Scrum framework has just enough structure to help teams plan frequently, work together to deliver something, inspect it, and adapt their plan, and talk about how they can do it better next time. That's what the five events of Scrum are all about. They create a feedback loop that helps the Scrum team learn. The artifacts make it clear what the plan for the product is, and who is doing what. Scrum includes artifacts like the Product Backlog and the Sprint Backlog that provide transparency on what the plan is for the product as well as the team's plan for delivering the Sprint. When you have visibility as to how work is proceeding in the Sprint Backlog, you can come up with ideas on how to improve your work process. And when you know what is in the Product Backlog and where the Product is going, you can better discuss what might be more valuable. Deliver early and often. When you deliver something, you learn a lot about feasibility and also whether it is what the customer really wanted. You're reducing business and technical risk and getting value sooner. When teams use Scrum, they deliver something usable every Sprint . Frequent delivery shortens the learning loop, so you get feedback faster and learn from it. Empiricism means learning by doing. Scrum isn't about just going through the motions. It's about using transparency as a tool that enables the team to inspect what was delivered and learn from it. The engine behind Scrum is Empiricism , a way to learn from experience and adapt based on what is learned. This doesn't get talked about enough. The superpower behind Scrum is that it is a learning engine when it's used effectively. Every artifact provides transparency, and every event is an opportunity to inspect and adapt. When you do that, you learn how to improve value delivery. A clear Product Goal promotes learning. The Scrum framework includes the establishment of a Product Goal. I worked with a consumer products company a few years back, and our Product Goal was to increase sales. The team met to discuss how to achieve it, and we decided to take two paths: increase traffic with SEO and decrease shopping cart abandonment. After every release, we measured the impact of our changes. Having a clear goal and being empowered to meet it meant we ran experiments to see what worked and what didn't. When you work towards a Product Goal, you learn over time what changes are a good step towards that goal, and which are not. And all of that adds up to a lot of learning and continuous improvement - but only when you realize that the framework was never the goal, but merely a means to an end. And that end is delivering value. Conclusion So no, most people will never use Calculus. But that was never the point. The point is learning how to learn. The Scrum framework is no different. When teams use Scrum, they learn how to work together effectively, how to deliver something of value, and they learn how to learn through experimentation and a focus on value delivery.

items.title: Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder
items.summary: Scientists discovered that vitamin B12 largely reversed developmental abnormalities in worms carrying a genetic mutation linked to Verheij syndrome, a rare disorder that causes growth problems and developmental delays. Similar metabolic changes were identified in human patients, raising the possibility that this common vitamin could inspire new treatments for rare genetic diseases.

items.title: NASA is offering $1 million for bold ideas to help build a Moon base
items.summary: NASA is offering $1 million in its new Moon Base Challenge, inviting U.S. students to develop innovative solutions for building humanity’s first permanent lunar outpost. items.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world
items.summary: A European spacecraft has revealed a mysterious, crater-covered side of the asteroid Didymos as it prepares to investigate the aftermath of NASA’s historic 2022 asteroid impact. The mission could uncover new clues about the collision and help turn asteroid deflection into a powerful defense against future threats to Earth.

items.title: The secret to building Moon bases may be hiding in emergency blankets
items.summary: Scientists have turned the thin plastic used in emergency blankets into remarkably strong insulation that could help astronauts survive the Moon's extreme temperatures. Built from hundreds of stacked layers, the material withstands crushing pressure without losing its thermal protection, potentially paving the way for tougher, longer-lasting lunar habitats.

items.title: Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that vitamin C may help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming in the stomach after eating foods containing nitrates and nitrites. A new mathematical model suggests that taking vitamin C after meals could reduce these harmful reactions, offering a possible new strategy for lowering cancer risk.

items.title: A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising genetic connection to spinal degeneration and found that an existing osteoporosis drug can prevent damaging mineral buildup in zebrafish spines. The discovery could pave the way for new treatments that slow or prevent a major cause of chronic back pain.

items.title: Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained
items.summary: The strange, wildly tilted magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune have puzzled scientists since NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft explored the planets in the 1980s. New simulations suggest that extreme conditions deep inside these icy giants create unusual electrical properties that could explain their magnetic fields. Remarkably, the models indicate that their magnetic poles could shift by tens of degrees within just a few decades, far faster than Earth's.

items.title: Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a strange stellar pair more than 5,000 light-years away, where a dead star spinning every eight minutes produces mysterious radio pulses while orbiting a Sun-like star. The breakthrough also revealed massive magnetic storms on the companion star, offering fresh clues to one of astronomy's emerging mysteries.

items.title: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections
items.summary: A surprising discovery from Rockefeller University suggests that a common amino acid could play a powerful role in protecting against cancer and viral infections. Scientists found that low arginine levels interfere with the immune system's ability to recognize dangerous cells, while increasing arginine intake reduced colon cancer tumors and improved viral infection outcomes in mice. Even more remarkably, giving mice arginine after they contracted influenza helped them recover.

items.title: Euclid discovers ancient cosmic beacons from the dawn of time, shining like a trillion suns
items.summary: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 ancient quasars, including two record-breaking objects that shone with the brightness of a trillion Suns when the Universe was just 670 million years old. Powered by supermassive black holes, these extraordinary cosmic beacons reveal a time when the first galaxies were still taking shape.

items.title: A new fiber supplement could help millions suffering from irritable bowel syndrome
items.summary: Scientists have developed a promising new fiber supplement that improves gut health in people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) without worsening bloating, pain, or other digestive symptoms. The specially designed blend also improved gut-related anxiety and produced surprisingly rapid changes in gut bacteria, potentially offering a new way to manage IBS.

items.title: A giant icy world hiding beyond Pluto could be our sixth dwarf planet
items.summary: Astronomers have uncovered a potentially enormous new dwarf planet beyond Pluto, hidden for years in one of the most crowded regions of the night sky. The discovery of 2026 ED138 could expand the solar system's official dwarf planet family and hints that more mysterious worlds may be lurking far beyond Neptune.

items.title: Yale scientists reveal what really slows aging and what doesn't
items.summary: Yale researchers have discovered that certain prescription drugs, healthy diets, and exercise can measurably slow biological aging, while popular anti-aging supplements appear largely ineffective. Their analysis of 51 studies could transform how scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments, although whether these biological changes actually extend life remains uncertain.
